title: Product quantization (PQ)
summary: How PQ compresses vectors with per-slice codebooks and scores codes by table lookups, and the methods built on it: IVF residuals, OPQ, 4-bit fast scan, ScaNN, additive quantizers and sizing.
outcomes: Explain why a product of m small codebooks gives (k*)^m centroids and compute a code's size in bits and bytes
Implement PQ training, encoding and ADC search in numpy and check it against Faiss
Explain why ADC beats SDC and decompose IVFADC distances into precomputable terms
Derive OPQ's Procrustes step and Eigenvalue Allocation, and judge when a rotation helps
Explain how 4-bit fast scan fits tables in SIMD registers and why it is paired with re-ranking

lessons.title: Why billion-vector indexes need compressed codes

blocks.md:
The previous course built product quantization by hand: split a vector into $m$ slices, give each slice a small k-means codebook, store the $m$ indices, and score a query against the codes with one per-query table of distances. It also measured the cost. On SIFT10K, Faiss `IndexPQ` kept 58.8, 72.1 and 84.1 percent recall@10 with 8, 16 and 32-byte codes (the raw vector is 512 bytes), and re-ranking a shortlist of 40 with exact distances lifted that to 89.4, 99.1 and 99.9 percent.

This course opens the box. It follows the original paper, **product quantization (PQ)** by Jegou, Douze and Schmid (TPAMI, the IEEE Transactions on Pattern Analysis and Machine Intelligence, 2011), then the work built on it: residual codes in inverted lists, learned rotations (OPQ), 4-bit fast scan, inner-product search with ScaNN's loss, additive quantizers, and how to size a real index.

First, why products at all. A **quantizer** maps a vector to the nearest of $k$ representative vectors, called **centroids**; the list of centroids is the **codebook**. Storing the centroid index costs $\log_2 k$ bits, because $b$ bits can count $2^b$ different indices (8 bits name 256 centroids).

The catch is scale. For a 64-bit code you need $k = 2^{64}$ centroids. The PQ paper points out that you cannot train that: k-means needs several times $k$ training samples, the cost is prohibitive, and there is not enough memory on Earth to store $2^{64}$ centroids.

blocks.prompt: Suppose you split a 128-dimensional vector into 8 chunks of 16 dimensions and give each chunk its own codebook of 256 centroids. How many distinct reconstructed vectors can the 8 codes describe, and how many centroids do you actually store?
blocks.reveal: The code picks one centroid per chunk independently, so it can describe $256^8 = 2^{64}$ distinct vectors. You only store $8 \times 256 = 2{,}048$ small centroids of 16 dimensions each. That gap, a huge implicit codebook built from a few small explicit ones, is the whole trick of product quantization.

blocks.md:
In the paper's notation, **product quantization** splits a $D$-dimensional vector into $m$ **sub-vectors** of $D^* = D/m$ dimensions each (so $D$ must be a multiple of $m$). Each sub-vector position $j$ gets its own small k-means codebook $C_j$ with $k^*$ centroids, called a **sub-quantizer**. A vector is stored as the $m$ indices of its nearest sub-centroids.

The full codebook is the Cartesian product $C = C_1 \times \dots \times C_m$, which is where the name comes from. A reconstructed vector is the concatenation of the chosen sub-centroids.

blocks.caption: Equation 8 of the PQ paper: each sub-vector u_j is quantized by its own sub-quantizer q_j.

blocks.title: Splitting an 8-dim vector into 4 sub-vectors and a 1-byte code

scenes.caption: A toy database vector y2 with D = 8 float32 values: 32 bytes. We will use m = 4 sub-vectors of D* = 2 dimensions and k* = 4 centroids per sub-quantizer.
Consecutive dimensions are grouped: dims 1-2 form u1, dims 3-4 form u2, and so on. Each group has its own codebook trained only on that slice of the data.
Each sub-vector is replaced by the index of its nearest centroid in its own codebook (next lesson computes these). y2 gets the code (2, 3, 2, 2).
With k* = 4, each index needs log2(4) = 2 bits, so the code is 4 x 2 = 8 bits = 1 byte, a 32x reduction. The 4 codebooks can jointly describe 4^4 = 256 different reconstructions.

blocks.tex: \text{code length} = m \log_2 k^* \text{ bits}, \qquad |C| = (k^*)^m, \qquad \text{codebook storage} = m\,k^*\,D^* = k^* D \text{ floats}
blocks.caption: The paper's resource counts, in words: a code takes m times log2 of k star bits, the m codebooks together describe k star to the power m vectors, and storing them takes m times k star times D star, which is k star times D floats. Codebook storage grows with k star but not with database size.

blocks.md:
The paper's usual setting is $k^* = 256$ (one byte per sub-vector) and $m = 8$, a 64-bit code. The paper tests on SIFT descriptors. SIFT (Scale-Invariant Feature Transform, Lowe 2004) describes a small image patch around a keypoint by histograms of gradient directions: 8 direction bins in each cell of a 4 by 4 grid, so 4 x 4 x 8 = 128 numbers. The standard benchmark, ANN_SIFT1M, holds 1 million of them. With $m = 8$ and $k^* = 256$, a 128-dim SIFT descriptor (512 bytes as float32) becomes 8 bytes, a 64x reduction. In Faiss the same thing is written `PQ8` (8 sub-quantizers, 8 bits each by default).

The plot below shows what this means at scale. Faiss's IVF variant (lesson 5) also stores an 8-byte id per vector, so we draw that too.

blocks.title: Index memory vs number of vectors

scenes.caption: At 1 billion vectors of 768 dims, raw float32 needs 3,072 GB; 64-byte PQ codes need 64 GB, or 72 GB with 8-byte ids. That is the difference between a cluster and one large server.
Shrinking codes to 16 bytes cuts memory 4x again (16 GB per billion codes), but recall drops as codes get shorter; lesson 10 turns this into a sizing procedure.
Simplified model: it counts only vectors or codes. Real indexes add codebooks, coarse centroids and list overhead, which are small next to the codes at this scale.

blocks.md: PQ builds an exponentially large codebook, $(k^*)^m$ centroids, out of $m$ tiny ones. Each vector costs $m \log_2 k^*$ bits no matter how many dimensions it has.

blocks.question: You use m = 16 sub-quantizers with k* = 256 on 512-dim float32 vectors. How many bytes does each PQ code take, and what is the compression ratio?
options: 16 bytes, 128x smaller than 2,048 bytes
256 bytes, 8x smaller
64 bytes, because each sub-vector stores 32 dims
2 bytes, because 16 codes x 1 bit
blocks.explain: Each of the 16 indices takes log2(256) = 8 bits = 1 byte, so 16 bytes. The raw vector is 512 x 4 = 2,048 bytes, so the ratio is 128x. The sub-vector width (32 dims) changes the codebook size, not the code size.

blocks.question: Why can't we just run k-means with 2^64 centroids to get 64-bit codes directly?
options: k-means only works in two dimensions
64-bit integers overflow on most CPUs
Training needs several times 2^64 samples and the centroids alone could not be stored
The resulting codes would be longer than 64 bits
blocks.explain: The PQ paper's argument: learning needs many more samples than centroids, the assignment cost scales with k, and storing D x 2^64 floats is impossible. Product quantization gets the same number of reproduction values from m small codebooks.

lessons.title: Training per-slice codebooks and encoding a vector

blocks.md:
Training a product quantizer is just **m independent k-means runs**. Take a training set, slice out sub-vector $j$ from every training vector, and run k-means with $k^*$ centroids on those slices. Repeat for each $j$. The cost is $m$ times one small k-means of $k^*$ centroids in $D^*$ dimensions.

k-means alternates two steps until it settles: assign each point to its nearest centroid, then move each centroid to the mean of its points. These are the two Lloyd optimality conditions the paper relies on. k-means only finds a local optimum, so results depend on the starting centroids.

Our toy: 40 training vectors of 8 dimensions, values rounded to one decimal, generated with a fixed random seed from a few clusters per 2-dim slice. We ran k-means with $k^* = 4$ on each of the 4 slices (numpy, fixed seed) and rounded the centroids to one decimal. Every number below is computed from those rounded values. For simplicity the toy database is the training set; real systems train on a separate sample.

Toy sizes hide one practical rule: k-means needs many points per centroid. Faiss's clustering warns when it gets fewer than 39 training vectors per centroid (`min_points_per_centroid` = 39) and subsamples above 256 per centroid. With $k^* = 256$ that means at least $39 \times 256 = 9{,}984$ training vectors, and the same vectors serve every slice. Training our toy's 40 vectors with $k^* = 256$ would be degenerate: more centroids than points. Lesson 4 measures what too little training data costs on real data.

blocks.title: The four learned codebooks (4 centroids of 2 dims each)

scenes.caption: Each row is one sub-quantizer: 4 centroids, each a 2-dim point (columns a and b). That is all the model we store: 4 x 4 x 2 = 32 floats, shared by every database vector.
Codebook u2 is crowded: its centroids lie within about 2.2 units of each other, while u3 spans more than 4 units. k-means adapts each codebook to the spread of its own slice.
Encoding y2 picks c2 in u1, c3 in u2, c2 in u3 and c2 in u4. Concatenating those cells gives the reconstruction q(y2).

blocks.md: **Encoding** a vector applies the first Lloyd condition per slice: for each $j$, compute the squared distance from $u_j(y)$ to each of the $k^*$ centroids of $C_j$ and keep the index of the smallest. The cost is $k^* D$ multiply-adds per vector, independent of the database size.

blocks.title: Encoding y2: squared distance to each centroid, per sub-vector

scenes.caption: u1(y2) = (0.5, 1.8). Distances to the u1 centroids: 7.25, 2.26, 0.05, 9.25. The nearest is c2 = (0.6, 1.6), so the first index is 2.
u2(y2) = (1.1, 0.1). Nearest is c3 = (1.3, -0.1) at 0.08, with c2 at 0.26 close behind. Index 3.
u3(y2) = (0.7, 2.5). c2 = (0.7, 2.0) wins at 0.25; c0 and c1 are far away. Index 2.
u4(y2) = (-0.3, 1.8). A close call: c2 at 0.13 beats c1 at 0.18. Index 2. The code for y2 is (2, 3, 2, 2).

blocks.title: Reconstruction and quantization error of y2

scenes.caption: The original vector. The index stores only the code (2, 3, 2, 2), so at search time the best we can know about y2 is its reconstruction.
q(y2) concatenates u1:c2, u2:c3, u3:c2, u4:c2. Close, but not equal.
Per-dimension squared error. The total is 0.51, about 3.5% of the squared norm of y2 (14.78). Over all 40 toy vectors the mean squared error is 1.03, versus a mean squared norm of 12.1.

blocks.md:
Squared distance is a sum over dimensions, and each dimension belongs to exactly one slice, so a vector's squared error splits into one term per slice. Because the sub-spaces are orthogonal, the total squared error is simply the sum of the per-slice errors: $\text{MSE}(q) = \sum_j \text{MSE}(q_j)$. This is why each codebook can be trained alone: minimizing each slice's k-means error minimizes the whole.

It also explains a weakness. A fixed $k^*$ per slice works best when every slice carries comparable energy (variance). If one slice holds most of the variance, its codebook is overloaded while others waste bits. The paper notes that consecutive components are often correlated and are better quantized together, so it keeps the natural order rather than shuffling dimensions; lesson 6 returns to this.

Common misconception: a PQ code is a lossless compression of the vector. It is not. Two different vectors with the same code are indistinguishable to the index, and every distance computed from codes inherits the quantization error.

blocks.question: A colleague trains one PQ codebook per sub-vector but forgets to use the same dimension split at encoding time (they split the database vectors in a different order). What happens?
options: Nothing, because k-means is permutation invariant
Codes are still valid but 2x larger
Every sub-vector is matched against a codebook learned on different dimensions, so reconstructions and distances are garbage
Only the first sub-vector is affected
blocks.explain: Codebook C_j only knows the distribution of slice j. Feeding it a different slice produces arbitrary nearest-centroid choices. The split (and any rotation applied before it) is part of the model and must be identical for training, encoding and querying.

blocks.question: For the same 64-bit budget on 128-dim SIFT, which setting did the PQ paper find gives lower quantization error?
options: m = 64 sub-quantizers with 2 centroids each
Both give exactly the same error because the bits are equal
m = 16 sub-quantizers with 16 centroids each
m = 8 sub-quantizers with 256 centroids each
blocks.explain: Figure 1 of the paper: for a fixed number of bits, fewer sub-quantizers with more centroids each give lower distortion, because each codebook captures more of the joint structure within its slice. The cost is that k* = 256 makes codebook training and table building more expensive than k* = 16 or 2. (16 x 16 is the 4-bit shape lesson 7 scans faster.)

lessons.title: Distances from codes: lookup tables, SDC and ADC

blocks.md:
Now the payoff: estimating distances without decompressing. The paper gives two estimators for the distance between a query $x$ and a database vector $y$.

- **Symmetric distance computation (SDC)**: quantize both, and use $d(q(x), q(y))$. Per sub-vector the squared distance between two centroids is read from a precomputed $k^* \times k^*$ table.
- **Asymmetric distance computation (ADC)**: quantize only the database vector, and use $d(x, q(y))$. The query stays exact.

blocks.caption: ADC (Equation 13), in words: the estimated squared distance is the sum, over the m slices, of the squared distance from the query's slice to the centroid the code picked for that slice. The m x k* slice-to-centroid distances are computed once per query.

blocks.md:
For ADC, the query preparation builds a **lookup table** (LUT) $T[j][i] = \|u_j(x) - c_{j,i}\|^2$: $m$ rows, $k^*$ columns, costing $k^* D$ operations once per query. Scoring a database code is then $m$ table reads and $m - 1$ additions. No vector arithmetic happens per database item, and square roots are skipped because they do not change the ranking.

Our toy query is $x = (0.2, 1.8, 0.8, -0.4, 0.5, 1.9, -1.1, 1.8)$.

blocks.title: ADC lookup table for query x (squared distances)

scenes.caption: Row j holds the squared distance from query slice u_j(x) to each centroid of codebook j. Example: u1(x) = (0.2, 1.8) vs c2 = (0.6, 1.6) gives 0.16 + 0.04 = 0.20. 16 numbers, computed once.
Score y2 with code (2, 3, 2, 2): read T[1][2] + T[2][3] + T[3][2] + T[4][2] = 0.20 + 0.34 + 0.05 + 1.25 = 1.84. The exact squared distance is 1.47.
Score y0 with code (0, 3, 2, 0): 5.78 + 0.34 + 0.05 + 4.05 = 10.22 (exact: 11.16). Same cost, 4 lookups, regardless of D.
Score y1 with code (2, 0, 3, 3): 0.20 + 2.89 + 2.61 + 7.25 = 12.95 (exact: 12.14). The ranking y2, y0, y1 matches the exact ranking.

blocks.title: The ADC scan loop

scenes.caption: The table is built once per query. The database is just small integer codes.
y0: four lookups summed. Its estimate 10.22 becomes the best so far.
y1 scores 12.95, which is worse, so the best is unchanged.
y2 scores 1.84 and wins. Real systems keep a max-heap of the K best instead of one best.

blocks.prompt: Now quantize the query too (SDC). x encodes to (2, 2, 2, 1). Using centroid-to-centroid tables, will the ranking of y0 (exact 11.16) and y1 (exact 12.14) stay correct?
blocks.reveal: No. SDC gives y0 = 7.54 + 0.50 + 0 + 4.21 = **12.25** and y1 = 0 + 2.41 + 2.18 + 4.81 = **9.40**, so y1 now looks closer than y0, which is wrong. Quantizing the query adds a second source of error. ADC kept the order (10.22 vs 12.95). Across all 40 toy vectors, SDC also swaps the 3rd and 4th true neighbors, while ADC's top 4 match the exact top 4.

blocks.title: Exact vs ADC vs SDC squared distances for 6 toy vectors

scenes.caption: Exact squared distances from x. True order: y2, y5, y0, y1, y3, y4.
ADC estimates: 10.22, 12.95, 1.84, 23.61, 31.00, 6.95. Off by up to 4 units, yet the order is preserved.
SDC estimates: 12.25, 9.40, 0.87, 25.20, 27.65, 4.96. y0 and y1 are now swapped: query quantization error broke the ranking.

blocks.md:
The paper bounds the error. The triangle inequality gives $|d(x,y) - d(x,q(y))| \le d(y,q(y))$: moving $y$ to its reconstruction cannot change its distance to $x$ by more than the move itself. Square and average over the database, and ADC's mean squared distance error is at most the quantizer's MSE. SDC moves both points, so its bound is $2 \times$ MSE. Both estimators are also **biased low** on average. Here is why for ADC: a k-means centroid $c$ is the mean of the vectors in its cell, so averaged over the vectors $y$ in that cell, $\|x - y\|^2 = \|x - c\|^2 + \|y - c\|^2$ (the cross term averages to zero). ADC keeps only the first term, so on average it falls short by the cell's mean squared error. The paper derives a correction term (this expected cell distortion) but finds it raises variance and gives worse search results, so it recommends the uncorrected estimator for ranking.

Empirically, on SIFT with $m = 8$, ADC with $k^* = 64$ matched SDC with $k^* = 256$, at the same speed. The only advantage of SDC is that the query is a code too, which rarely matters.
ADC = exact query, quantized database. Per query you build an $m \times k^*$ table once, then each database vector costs $m$ lookups and adds. This is why PQ scans are fast and why everyone uses ADC.

blocks.question: With m = 8 and k* = 256, how many table entries does the ADC lookup table hold per query, and how many lookups score one database vector?
options: 2,048 entries, 8 lookups
256 entries, 256 lookups
65,536 entries, 8 lookups
8 entries, 256 lookups
blocks.explain: The table has m x k* = 8 x 256 = 2,048 entries (one per sub-quantizer and centroid). Each database code has 8 indices, so scoring it reads 8 entries. The 256 x 256 = 65,536 figure is the size of one SDC centroid-to-centroid table.

blocks.question: Your ADC distances are consistently smaller than the true distances. Is that a bug?
options: Yes: ADC should be unbiased because the query is exact
Yes: you forgot the square roots
No: the paper shows the estimator underestimates on average, and ranking does not need the bias removed
No: but you must add the correction term or recall collapses
blocks.explain: Jegou et al. show d(x, q(y)) underestimates on average. Adding the expected distortion removes the bias but increases variance, and in their experiments the corrected version gave inferior search results. Correct it only if you need the distance values themselves, for example for a radius threshold.

lessons.title: Write PQ from scratch in numpy, then check it against Faiss

blocks.md: You can now write the whole method yourself. The surprise is how little code it takes: about 30 lines of numpy for training, encoding and ADC search. Writing it shows the one fact that explains every fast PQ scanner: scoring a code is a **gather** (read one table entry per slice, chosen by the code) followed by a **sum**. No vector arithmetic touches the database at search time.

blocks.caption: pq_numpy.py, the code we ran. train is m independent k-means runs (20 Lloyd iterations, random starting centroids); encode is an argmin per slice; adc_search builds the m x ks table and scores every code at once.

blocks.md: Read `adc_search` line by line. `q.reshape(m, 1, ds) - cb` broadcasts the query's $m$ slices against all $k^*$ centroids of the matching codebook, so the table has shape $m \times k^*$. `lut[np.arange(m), codes]` is numpy fancy indexing: for every database row it picks entry `codes[i, j]` from row `j`, giving an $n \times m$ array of looked-up numbers. Summing each row gives the $n$ ADC estimates. `np.argpartition` finds the $k$ smallest without sorting all $n$, then only those $k$ are sorted.

blocks.title: The vectorized ADC scan on lesson 3's toy
blocks.code:
import numpy as np
cb = np.array(CODEBOOKS)    # lesson 2: m=4, ks=4, ds=2
codes = np.array([[0, 3, 2, 0],    # y0
                  [2, 0, 3, 3],    # y1
                  [2, 3, 2, 2]])   # y2
q = np.array([0.2, 1.8, 0.8, -0.4, 0.5, 1.9, -1.1, 1.8])
m, ks, ds = cb.shape
lut = ((q.reshape(m, 1, ds) - cb) ** 2).sum(-1)
g = lut[np.arange(m), codes]       # gather: shape (3, 4)
est = g.sum(1)
k = 2
top = np.argpartition(est, k)[:k]
top = top[np.argsort(est[top])]
print(top, est[top].round(2))

scenes.caption: Same toy as lesson 3: the four codebooks, three stored codes and query x. Nothing about the database is a float vector any more.
One broadcast builds the 4 x 4 table: row j holds the squared distances from the query's slice j to the 4 centroids of codebook j.
The gather: row i of g holds the 4 table entries chosen by code i. y2's row is 0.20, 0.34, 0.05, 1.25.
Sum each row: 10.22, 12.95 and 1.84, the same ADC estimates lesson 3 added up by hand.
argpartition keeps the 2 smallest without a full sort, then those 2 are ordered: y2 first, then y0.

blocks.md: Now real data. We ran `pq_numpy.py` on SIFT10K, the 10,000-vector SIFT benchmark from the previous course: codebooks trained on its 25,000-vector learning set, 100 queries, exhaustive search, recall@10 measured as the overlap between the returned 10 and the true 10 (the previous course's metric). Then we ran Faiss `IndexPQ` with the same $m$ and $k^* = 256$, and measured SDC both ways, using a $k^* \times k^*$ centroid-to-centroid table per slice.

scenes.caption: ADC. Numpy: 56.8, 70.9 and 82.8 percent for 8, 16 and 32-byte codes. Faiss (the previous course's numbers): 58.8, 72.1 and 84.1.
SDC on the same codes. Numpy 45.6, 64.5, 77.3; Faiss 46.7, 66.3, 78.5. Quantizing the query costs 5 to 12 points here, most with the shortest codes.

blocks.md:
Our version lands 1.2 to 2.0 points below Faiss at every size. That gap is the size you expect from k-means details: Faiss runs 25 iterations by default (we ran 20) and starts from a different random draw of training points. Our reconstruction MSE on the base set was 11,193 for 16 bytes against 11,168 for Faiss, almost the same codebooks.

The SDC rows are lesson 3's argument measured on real data: lesson 3's toy ranking swap becomes a 6-point recall loss at 16 bytes.

blocks.prompt: Train the 16-byte numpy PQ on only 300 learning vectors instead of 25,000, with $k^* = 256$. Faiss would print a warning. How much recall@10 do you expect to lose?
blocks.reveal: Less than you might fear, but it is still a mistake. With 300 vectors, k-means starts from 256 of them, so almost every centroid is one training point. Recall@10 fell from 70.9 to **67.6** percent (with 2,000 vectors it was 70.6). Faiss on the same 300 vectors prints `WARNING clustering 300 points to 256 centroids: please provide at least 9984 training points`, which is 39 x 256. This is one run on one dataset; data that drifts away from a small training sample can lose more.

blocks.question: A colleague's from-scratch PQ16 gets 0.0 percent recall@10 on SIFT10K while Faiss gets 72.1 on the same data. Which bug fits that number best?
options: They train on 2,000 instead of 25,000 vectors
They encode database vectors with their slices in a different order than the codebooks were trained on
They score with SDC instead of ADC
They skip the square root when computing distances
blocks.explain: We tried it: reversing the slice order at encoding time gave exactly 0.0 percent, because every slice is matched against a codebook learned on other dimensions. Training on 2,000 vectors cost 0.3 points (70.6 vs 70.9), SDC about 6 points (64.5), and the square root never changes a ranking.

blocks.md: ADC is a gather plus a sum: `lut[np.arange(m), codes].sum(1)`. Once that clicks, every fast PQ kernel is the same loop made cheaper: smaller tables (lesson 7), fewer codes scanned (lesson 5) or better codes (lessons 6 and 9).

lessons.title: IVFADC: inverted lists with residual codes

blocks.md:
ADC still touches every code. At a billion vectors and 8 lookups each, that is 8 billion lookups per query. The paper's fix is **IVFADC**: an inverted file with asymmetric distance computation.

A **coarse quantizer** $q_c$ is an ordinary k-means with $k'$ centroids (the paper uses $k'$ from 1,000 to 1,000,000 for SIFT). It partitions the database into $k'$ **inverted lists**. The name comes from text search, where an inverted index stores, for each word, the list of documents that contain it; here each coarse centroid stores the ids and codes of the vectors assigned to it. A query scans only the lists of its $w$ nearest coarse centroids, about $n \times w / k'$ entries for a database of $n$ vectors when lists are balanced. Faiss calls $k'$ `nlist` and $w$ `nprobe`.

The second idea is to encode the **residual** instead of the vector:

$r(y) = y - q_c(y)$

The residual has much less energy than the vector itself, so the same PQ budget describes it more precisely. The paper's analogy: the coarse centroid supplies the most significant bits, the PQ code the least significant ones. One product quantizer is trained on residuals pooled from all cells, rather than one per cell, which would cost $k' \times D \times k^*$ floats.

scenes.caption: Indexing: y is assigned to its nearest coarse centroid, the residual is PQ-encoded, and (id, code) is appended to that centroid's list. The query path is hidden for now.
Why residuals: y minus its coarse centroid is small, so the PQ codebooks (trained on residuals from all cells) spend their bits on fine detail instead of on which region y lives in.
Search: the query finds its w nearest coarse centroids (multiple assignment). The database is not multiply assigned, which would multiply memory.
For each probed list, the query residual x - qc changes, so a fresh m x k* table is built per list. Then only that list's codes are scanned.
Each estimated distance enters a fixed-size max-heap only if it beats the current K-th best. Only the scan step grows with the database.

blocks.caption: Equation 31 in words: subtract y's coarse centroid from the query, then sum over slices the squared distance from that query residual's slice to the centroid stored in y's residual code (q_p,j is slice j of the product quantizer trained on residuals).

blocks.md: GIST (Oliva and Torralba, 2001) is a global image descriptor: it summarizes a whole picture by how strongly oriented edge filters respond at several scales in each cell of a 4 by 4 grid; the color version used here has 960 numbers. The paper's GIST experiment (1M vectors, 960 dims, 64-bit codes, 500 queries) shows the effect. The paper's recall@100 is not the overlap measure from the previous course: it is the fraction of queries whose single true nearest neighbor appears among the first 100 results. Exhaustive ADC compared 1,000,991 codes in 17.2 ms per query with recall@100 of 0.652. IVFADC with $k' = 1024, w = 8$ compared only 27,818 codes in 8.8 ms and reached 0.682, because residual codes are more accurate. With $w = 1$ it took 1.5 ms but recall fell to 0.308: the true neighbor often sits in a nearby cell, and a neighbor in an unvisited list is lost for good.

nprobe = 4 (9.9% scanned): 0.42, 0.71, 0.88, 0.96. Simplified: synthetic 64-dim data with well-separated clusters (20,000 vectors, 500 queries), so one list already holds most true neighbors; real data needs larger nprobe.

blocks.md: In Faiss this is `IndexIVFPQ(quantizer, d, nlist, M, nbits)`, or the factory string `IVF4096,PQ16`. Faiss calls this index IVFPQ and writes $m$ as `M`, the bits per sub-quantizer (log2 of the centroid count) as `nbits` and the centroid count as `ksub`; `d` is the dimension $D$. A factory string is a short text recipe that `faiss.index_factory` turns into an index: `IVF4096` means 4096 inverted lists and `PQ16` means 16 sub-quantizers. Encoding by residual is the default (`by_residual = true`). Each stored entry costs the code, ceil(M x nbits / 8) bytes, plus an 8-byte id. With L2 distance a precomputed table (`use_precomputed_table`, size nlist x M x ksub) speeds up building the per-list tables at some memory cost; here is why it works.

blocks.tex: \|x - y_C - y_R\|^2 = \underbrace{\|x - y_C\|^2}_{\text{term 1}} + \underbrace{\|y_R\|^2 + 2\langle y_C, y_R\rangle}_{\text{term 2}} \underbrace{- 2\langle x, y_R\rangle}_{\text{term 3}}
blocks.caption: The decomposition in Faiss's IndexIVFPQ.cpp. x is the query, y_C the coarse centroid of the list, y_R the PQ reconstruction of the residual. Expand the square and group the terms by what they depend on.

blocks.md:
Each term depends on different things, so each is paid at a different time:

- **Term 1** is the query's distance to the coarse centroid. The coarse search already computed it, once per probed list.
- **Term 2** involves no query. Because $y_R$ is a concatenation of sub-centroids, it splits into one number per list, slice and centroid, so it can be stored as a table of nlist x M x ksub floats, built once.
- **Term 3** is $-2$ times an inner product with the same sub-centroids for every list: one $M \times$ ksub table per query, not per list.

Per probed list, the scanner adds the stored term-2 table to the query's term-3 table instead of building a fresh distance table. Faiss's comment says this pays off when lists are longer than ksub x M. Faiss turns it on automatically for L2 with residuals when the table fits under `precomputed_table_max_bytes`, 2 GiB by default.

We checked the identity on a real index: SIFT10K, `IVF100,PQ16`, the first query and its top result, which sits in list 68. Term 1 is 74,844.37, term 2 is 80,446.50 and term 3 is -81,162.32. They sum to 74,128.55, exactly the directly computed $\|x - y_C - y_R\|^2$ and exactly the distance Faiss returned. The true squared distance is 77,004, so this estimate is 3.7 percent low, in line with the bias from lesson 3.

blocks.code:
import faiss, numpy as np

d, nlist, M, nbits = 768, 4096, 64, 8
xt = np.random.rand(200_000, d).astype('float32')  # training sample
xb = np.random.rand(1_000_000, d).astype('float32')

quantizer = faiss.IndexFlatL2(d)            # coarse quantizer
index = faiss.IndexIVFPQ(quantizer, d, nlist, M, nbits)
index.train(xt)       # k-means for coarse centroids, then PQ on residuals
index.add(xb)         # 64-byte code + 8-byte id per vector

index.nprobe = 16     # w: lists scanned per query
D, I = index.search(xb[:5], 10)
blocks.caption: IVFADC in Faiss. Equivalent factory: faiss.index_factory(768, "IVF4096,PQ64"). Random data is only a placeholder.

blocks.md: Raising code size cannot fix a too-small nprobe. The paper notes that increasing the code length is useless if w is not big enough, because neighbors outside the probed lists are never scored. Tune nprobe first, then code size.

blocks.question: An IVFPQ index with nlist = 1024 and PQ64 has poor recall. Profiling shows the true nearest neighbor is usually in the 3rd or 4th nearest list. Which change helps most?
options: Switch to PQ128 codes
Reduce nlist to 64 so lists are bigger
Turn off residual encoding
Increase nprobe from 1 to 8
blocks.explain: Neighbors in unprobed lists are never scored, so better codes cannot find them. Raising nprobe scans those lists. Shrinking nlist also captures them but scans a much larger fraction per probe; the paper finds that for a fixed fraction visited, more lists with more probes is more accurate.

blocks.question: Why does IVFADC build a new lookup table for each probed list instead of one table per query?
options: Each list has its own PQ codebook
The codes are encoded relative to that list's coarse centroid, so the query residual x - qc changes per list
Faiss recomputes tables to avoid cache misses
The table depends on the database vector id
blocks.explain: The stored codes describe y - qc(y). To compare, the query must be expressed relative to the same centroid, x - qc. The codebook is shared across lists, but the query sub-vectors differ, so the m x k* distances differ.

lessons.title: OPQ: rotating the space before you split it

blocks.md: Lesson 2 ended on a weakness: PQ cuts the dimensions into fixed consecutive slices, and every slice gets the same $k^*$ centroids whether it carries most of the variance or almost none. Why it matters: the PQ paper itself showed the split has a big effect. On GIST with $m = 8$, ADC recall@100 was 0.338 with the natural order, 0.286 with a random order and 0.652 with a structured order that groups related histogram bins. OPQ learns such a grouping instead of relying on prior knowledge.

A 4-dimensional toy makes the problem concrete. We drew 2,000 Gaussian points whose standard deviations are 3, 2, 0.5 and 0.3, rotated dimensions 1 and 2 by 30 degrees so they are correlated, and quantized with $m = 2$ slices of 2 dimensions and $k^* = 4$ centroids each (a 4-bit code). The natural split puts both big dimensions in slice 1: its variance is 12.90, slice 2 holds 0.35. Every number here comes from a numpy script with a fixed seed. The figure's second scene previews the fix, PCA plus Eigenvalue Allocation, explained just below it.

blocks.title: Covariance of the toy, before and after the OPQ rotation

scenes.caption: Natural order. The top-left 2 x 2 block (slice 1) holds almost all the variance and is correlated (2.14 off the diagonal). Slice 2's 4 centroids are spent on almost nothing.

After PCA and Eigenvalue Allocation: off-diagonal terms are 0 (independence) and each slice pairs a large eigenvalue with a small one, 9.09 with 0.09 and 3.81 with 0.26. Products 0.84 and 0.98: balanced.

blocks.md:
The parametric method assumes Gaussian data: align by PCA (principal component analysis, which rotates the data onto the eigenvectors of its covariance matrix; each eigenvalue is the variance along its direction), then greedily assign eigenvalues to $m$ buckets so the product of eigenvalues per sub-space is balanced (**Eigenvalue Allocation**).

Why products: for Gaussian data the OPQ paper bounds a sub-space's distortion by a term that grows with the product of its eigenvalues (the $D^*$-th root of that product). The product over all sub-spaces is fixed by the data, so the sum of the bounds is smallest when every sub-space gets the same product. The greedy rule sorts eigenvalues from largest to smallest and gives each to the bucket with the smallest product so far that still has room.

blocks.caption: OPQ paper, Eqs. 13 to 15 (M here is the course's m). Sigma_mm: sub-space m's covariance; |.|: determinant. Step 1, the AM-GM inequality (arithmetic mean at least geometric mean), is tight when determinants match; step 2, Fischer's inequality, when sub-spaces are uncorrelated.

blocks.md: On the toy the greedy rule runs in four steps. Sorted eigenvalues: 9.09, 3.81, 0.26, 0.09. The first two go to the two empty buckets. 0.26 goes to the bucket with the smaller product (3.81), and 0.09 to the only bucket with room. The rotation $R$ is the eigenvectors reordered into those buckets.

blocks.title: Toy PQ distortion (mean squared error) by rotation

scenes.caption: Natural split: 4.21, a third of the total variance of 13.25. PCA with eigenvalues in sorted order gives the same 4.21, because it puts the two big directions back into one slice.
PCA plus Eigenvalue Allocation: 1.83, less than half. Same codebook sizes and code length; only the split changed.

blocks.md: **OPQ (Optimized Product Quantization)**, Ge, He, Ke and Sun (CVPR 2013, the IEEE Conference on Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition), attacks the dimension-split problem from lesson 2. It learns an orthogonal rotation $R$ applied before PQ, jointly with the codebooks, to minimize quantization distortion. A rotation is safe because it preserves lengths and angles: distances and inner products between rotated vectors equal those between the originals, so the nearest neighbors do not change. It only decides which directions land in which slice. The non-parametric method alternates: fix $R$ and run PQ k-means; fix the codebooks and solve for $R$ in closed form with an SVD (an orthogonal Procrustes problem). Procrustes asks for the rotation that best maps one point set onto another, here the vectors onto their PQ reconstructions. The singular value decomposition (SVD) factors the matrix $X Y^\top$ (vectors times reconstructions) into rotation, scaling, rotation, $U S V^\top$, and the best rotation is $R = V U^\top$: the two rotations with the scaling dropped.

blocks.tex: \|RX - Y\|_F^2 = \|X\|_F^2 + \|Y\|_F^2 - 2\,\mathrm{tr}(R\,XY^\top), \quad XY^\top = USV^\top \;\Rightarrow\; \mathrm{tr}(R\,USV^\top) = \mathrm{tr}(V^\top R U\, S) \le \textstyle\sum_i s_i
blocks.caption: The Procrustes step derived (F: Frobenius norm, root of the sum of squared entries; tr: trace, sum of the diagonal). Rotations keep norms, so only the trace term depends on R. Z = V^T R U is orthogonal, so tr(ZS) is at most the sum of singular values, reached at Z = I, that is R = V U^T.

blocks.md: We ran the non-parametric loop on the toy, starting from no rotation and re-running k-means (25 Lloyd iterations from a fresh start) at every step. The paper's cheaper variant, one warm-started k-means pass per step, follows the same path more slowly and reaches 1.83 by iteration 15. Through iteration 6 distortion barely moves (4.21 to 4.14): the codebooks fit the bad split and the rotation only nudges it. Then it escapes, 4.02 at iteration 7, 2.83 at 9, and settles at 1.83, the value Eigenvalue Allocation reached in one shot. That is why the paper uses the parametric solution to initialize the loop. Faiss's `OPQMatrix` runs 50 outer iterations and starts from a random rotation.

blocks.title: Non-parametric OPQ on the toy: distortion by iteration

scenes.caption: Iterations 0 to 6: the alternation is stuck near the natural split's 4.21.
Iterations 7 to 10: the rotation turns far enough that k-means reassigns, and distortion collapses to 1.83, where it stays through iteration 20.

blocks.md: Now SIFT10K with 16-byte codes. SIFT's natural order is already good: consecutive dimensions are histograms of neighboring grid cells, and in the PQ paper's Table IV (SIFT, m = 8) the natural order reached recall@100 0.921, against 0.905 structured and 0.859 random. So we tried five splits: natural; a random rotation (`RR128,PQ16`); Faiss's `OPQ16,PQ16`, which starts from a random rotation; PCA with Eigenvalue Allocation; and our numpy non-parametric loop started from no rotation (10 iterations). Each was scored by Faiss `IndexPQ` on the rotated data, 100 queries.

blocks.title: SIFT10K, 16-byte codes: recall@10 (%) by rotation

scenes.caption: Recall@10: natural 72.1, random rotation 59.1, Faiss OPQ 70.4, PCA plus allocation 70.9, OPQ from natural 74.1. That last bar is a tie, not a win: the same loop gave 73.6 after one step and 73.4 and 72.9 after 20 and 30, within the noise of 100 queries.

Base-set reconstruction MSE (thousands): 11.2, 30.7, 16.9, 15.5 and 10.8. The random rotation destroys SIFT's slice structure; Faiss's OPQ recovers most but not all of it in 50 iterations. OPQ from natural trims MSE by only 3 percent.

blocks.md: On the synthetic set that lesson 10 describes (randomly rotated, so slices were already balanced) the parametric OPQ rotation lowered MSE from 1.92 to 1.71 at 8 bytes and moved 1-recall@10 from 0.42 to 0.44: a modest gain when variance is already spread out. In Faiss, prefix the factory string with `OPQ16` or `OPQ16_64` (rotate for 16 sub-quantizers and reduce to 64 dims). On SIFT10K the matching prefix (OPQ8, OPQ16, OPQ32) scored lower at every size we tried: 54.5 vs 58.8 percent at 8 bytes, 70.4 vs 72.1 at 16 and 81.5 vs 84.1 at 32, with higher MSE each time. One gap alone is near the noise of 100 queries; all three point the same way. The Faiss guide still recommends OPQ for memory-bound indexes, with an output dimension $D$ that is a multiple of $M$, at most the input dimension and preferably $D = 4M$.

blocks.code:
import faiss

# rotate for 16 sub-quantizers and reduce 128 to 64 dims, then PQ16
index = faiss.index_factory(128, "OPQ16_64,PQ16")
index.train(xt)            # learns the OPQ matrix, then the codebooks
index.add(xb)
D, I = index.search(xq, 10)

# the same pieces by hand
opq = faiss.OPQMatrix(128, 16)   # niter = 50 outer iterations by default
pq = faiss.IndexPQ(128, 16, 8)
index2 = faiss.IndexPreTransform(opq, pq)

# always compare against the same PQ without OPQ
base = faiss.index_factory(128, "PQ16")
blocks.caption: Faiss OPQ two ways. On SIFT10K, OPQ16_64,PQ16 also gave 70.4 percent recall@10, the same as OPQ16 without the dimension reduction.

blocks.md: OPQ is not a free win. It helps when variance is concentrated in a few directions or spread unevenly across slices, and it can lose when the natural order already groups related dimensions, as on SIFT. Measure recall with and without it on your data.

blocks.question: You apply OPQ to embeddings that were already PCA-whitened (every direction rescaled to variance 1). Recall barely moves. Why?
options: OPQ only works on image descriptors
Whitening breaks the orthogonality OPQ needs
Every eigenvalue is now equal, so every split already has the same eigenvalue product and there is nothing to balance
OPQ needs more than 16 sub-quantizers to have any effect
blocks.explain: Eigenvalue Allocation balances products of eigenvalues across sub-spaces. After whitening they are all 1, so any rotation gives the same bound. We tried it on whitened SIFT10K: PQ16 53.9 percent recall@10, OPQ16 54.8. What is left is the non-Gaussian structure the bound ignores.

blocks.question: Your embeddings come from a model whose first 32 of 256 dimensions carry most of the variance. Plain PQ with M = 16 has poor recall. What is the most targeted fix?
options: Increase nprobe
Apply an OPQ rotation before PQ so variance is balanced across sub-spaces
Switch from ADC to SDC
Use k* = 16 instead of 256
blocks.explain: With the natural split, the first 2 sub-quantizers must represent most of the variance with 256 centroids each, while the rest waste bits. OPQ learns a rotation (for Gaussian data, Eigenvalue Allocation balances eigenvalue products) so each sub-space gets comparable energy. nprobe only matters for IVF list coverage.

lessons.title: PQ fast scan: 4-bit codes, SIMD lookups and 8-bit tables

blocks.md: Lesson 4 showed that a PQ scan is a gather plus a sum. With $k^* = 256$, every gather is a read from a table of 256 floats (1 KB per sub-quantizer) that lives in L1 cache (the CPU's smallest and fastest cache): fast, but still one memory access per sub-quantizer per vector. Modern CPUs do arithmetic on registers much faster than they do lookups in memory. 4-bit codes can be scored with SIMD (single instruction, multiple data) instructions, where one CPU instruction works on many values packed in a wide register. **Fast scan** moves the lookup tables themselves into SIMD registers.

The idea comes from Andre, Kermarrec and Le Scouarnec (VLDB 2015, the Very Large Data Bases conference), titled *Cache locality is not enough*. Their PQ Fast Scan kept ordinary 8 x 8-bit codes and built small 16-entry tables from the big ones (by grouping vectors that share code prefixes and by taking minimums), quantized to 8 bits so that a table fits one 128-bit register. Those small tables give lower bounds that prune most vectors, so the answers are the same as plain PQ, with 4 to 6 times lower response time (74 ms to 13 ms on 25 million vectors).

The same authors' Quick ADC (ICMR 2017, the ACM International Conference on Multimedia Retrieval) took the shorter road: 4-bit sub-quantizers ($k^* = 16$), so the tables are 16 entries long to begin with, plus 8-bit quantized distances. Faiss's fast scan, which its wiki says is heavily inspired by Google's ScaNN, uses that 4-bit design.

blocks.title: Why 4-bit codes fit a SIMD register lookup

scenes.caption: With k* = 256, one sub-quantizer's table row has 256 float entries (1 KB), read from cache with one lookup per code. Fast scan cannot use this layout.
With k* = 16, the row has 16 entries; quantized to 8-bit integers it is exactly 128 bits. Values shown are illustrative, not from a real query.

A shuffle instruction treats a register of 4-bit codes as indices into the in-register table, looking up many vectors at once. Here code 2 reads position 2 (value 0) and code 7 reads position 7 (value 5).

blocks.md: The tables must also be small in bits: 16 floats are 512 bits, too wide. So after building the float table for a query, Faiss rounds it to unsigned 8-bit integers. Its rule (`quantize_lut.cpp`): subtract each sub-quantizer's own minimum, multiply every entry by one shared scale $a$, round. The minimums are added back as a single bias $b$. The scale is the largest that keeps every entry within 0 to 255 and the sum of $M$ entries within the 16-bit range, so sums are accumulated in 16-bit integers without overflow.

blocks.tex: \mathrm{LUT}_8[j][i] = \big\lfloor a\,(T[j][i] - \min_i T[j][i]) + 0.5 \big\rfloor, \qquad \tilde d \approx \frac{1}{a}\sum_j \mathrm{LUT}_8[j][c_j] + b, \quad b = \sum_j \min_i T[j][i]
blocks.caption: Per-table offset, one shared scale. a = min(255 / largest span, about 65535 / sum of spans); the floor of x + 0.5 rounds to the nearest integer.

blocks.title: Lesson 3's lookup table, before and after 8-bit quantization

scenes.caption: The float table for query x from lesson 3. Row minimums are 0.20, 0.20, 0.05 and 0.34 (b = 0.79); the widest row span is row 3's 15.17.
Quantized with a = 255 / 15.17 = 16.81. Each row now starts at 0, and the widest row reaches exactly 255. In real fast scan each 16-entry row of such bytes fills one 128-bit register.
Scoring y2 = (2, 3, 2, 2) reads 0 + 2 + 0 + 15 = 17. Dividing by a and adding b gives 1.80, against the float score 1.84.

blocks.title: Float vs 8-bit table scores for the three toy codes

scenes.caption: Float ADC scores from lesson 3: 10.22, 12.95, 1.84.
From the 8-bit table: 10.19, 12.93, 1.80. Each lookup is off by at most 0.5 / a = 0.03, so 4 lookups by at most 0.12. Same ranking. Simplified: a real fast-scan table has 16 columns, not 4.

blocks.md: The codes are rearranged too. Faiss packs them in **blocks of 32 vectors** (`bbs = 32`): each 32-byte chunk holds the 4-bit codes of 2 sub-quantizers for all 32 vectors, so one load brings in exactly the indices one shuffle needs. A shuffle instruction (such as `pshufb` on x86, the one Andre et al. used) treats the register of codes as indices into the register holding a 16-entry table and returns all the looked-up bytes at once. The 8-bit results are widened and added into 16-bit accumulators. For IVF, a per-list 16-bit bias carries the coarse term, as in lesson 5. The Faiss wiki says the kernel is geared towards AVX (x86's 256-bit SIMD instructions) but Arm Neon (Arm's 128-bit SIMD instructions) is also supported, which is why it runs on the Apple Silicon Mac we used.

blocks.title: Fast-scan code layout, M = 8 sub-quantizers, one block of 32 vectors

scenes.caption: One block covers 32 vectors. Its codes occupy M / 2 = 4 chunks of 32 bytes; 32 bytes x 4 = 128 bytes = 32 vectors x 8 codes x 4 bits.
Chunk 0 holds sub-quantizers 0 and 1 for all 32 vectors. With masking and shifting, two shuffles fetch the 2 x 32 table entries this chunk needs.
The next chunk serves sub-quantizers 2 and 3, and so on. After 4 chunks, 32 distances sit in 16-bit accumulators and the next block starts.

blocks.prompt: PQ32x4 and PQ32x4fs use the same 4-bit codebooks; only fast scan rounds the tables to 8 bits. Both are 16 bytes per vector, like PQ16 (8-bit). On SIFT10K, where do you expect the big recall gap: between PQ16 and PQ32x4, or between PQ32x4 and PQ32x4fs?
blocks.reveal: Between PQ16 and PQ32x4. We measured recall@10 of **72.1** for PQ16, **61.1** for PQ32x4 and **61.1** for PQ32x4fs. Rounding the tables cost nothing measurable here; giving each sub-quantizer only 16 centroids is what costs 11 points. That matches the Faiss wiki: PQ32x4 is significantly less accurate than PQ16x8 at the same memory.

blocks.title: SIFT10K, 16 bytes per vector: recall@10 (%)

scenes.caption: Codes alone: PQ16 72.1, PQ32x4 61.1, PQ32x4fs 61.1.
Re-ranking a shortlist of 40 with exact distances (k_factor = 4): 99.1, 93.5, 93.3.
A shortlist of 100 (k_factor = 10): 100, 99.7, 99.7. With re-ranking, the 4-bit codes only need to get true neighbors into a longer shortlist.

blocks.title: SIFT1M exhaustive scan, one thread: milliseconds per query

scenes.caption: 1 million codes of 16 bytes, 200 queries in one batch, one thread on this Apple Silicon Mac (other jobs were running, so read the ratios). PQ16: 2.91 ms. PQ32x4fs: 0.51 ms, 5.7 times faster.

PQ32x4 without fast scan took 20.61 ms: unpacking 4-bit codes one by one is slower than byte lookups. The 4-bit layout only pays off with the in-register kernel. Recall@10 on SIFT1M: 54.2 for PQ16, 40.8 for PQ32x4fs.

blocks.code:
import faiss

# 4-bit fast scan, 16 bytes per vector, exact re-ranking of k * k_factor candidates
index = faiss.index_factory(128, "PQ32x4fs,RFlat")
index.train(xt)
index.add(xb)
index.k_factor = 4
D, I = index.search(xq, 10)

# IVF variant with residual encoding (fsr) and an SQ8 refine stage
ivf = faiss.index_factory(128, "IVF1024,PQ32x4fsr,Refine(SQ8)")
blocks.caption: The factory strings from the Faiss FastScan wiki. RFlat keeps the float vectors in RAM; Refine(SQ8) keeps 1 byte per dimension instead.

blocks.md: Fast scan trades codebook size for speed: 16-entry tables fit in a register and are looked up 32 vectors at a time. Rounding the tables to 8 bits costs almost nothing; the 4-bit codebooks cost real recall, so fast scan is normally paired with re-ranking.

blocks.question: A 4-bit fast-scan index (PQ32x4fs) and an 8-bit index (PQ16) both use 16 bytes per vector. Which statement matches the Faiss docs?
options: Fast scan is faster but less accurate than 8-bit PQ at the same memory, so pair it with re-ranking
They are identical because the bytes are equal
Fast scan is more accurate because it has more sub-quantizers
Fast scan stores float32 tables in registers
blocks.explain: Faiss notes 4-bit PQ is less accurate than 8-bit PQ for the same memory and recommends a refine stage. Its speed comes from 16-entry tables quantized to 8-bit integers, which fit in SIMD registers.

blocks.question: Fast scan accumulates 8-bit table entries in 16-bit integers. With M = 64 sub-quantizers, why can the sum never overflow?
options: Because the CPU saturates at 65,535 and that is harmless
Because fast scan only supports M up to 16
Because 64 x 255 is below 65,535, and Faiss chooses the scale so the sum of the table spans fits as well
Because the codes are 4 bits, so each entry is at most 15
blocks.explain: Each entry is at most 255, and 64 x 255 = 16,320, comfortably within 16 bits. Faiss picks the scale a as the smaller of 255 / (largest table span) and about 65,535 / (sum of spans), so even very large M cannot overflow; the price is coarser rounding. The 4 bits are the indices, not the table values.

lessons.title: Inner product, cosine and ScaNN's anisotropic quantization

blocks.md: Text and image embeddings are usually compared by **inner product** (the dot product $\langle x, y \rangle$, larger means more similar) or by **cosine similarity**, the inner product of the two vectors after scaling each to length 1. Everything so far used squared L2 distance. Tiny example: for unit vectors $x = (1, 0)$ and $y = (0.6, 0.8)$, $\langle x, y\rangle = 0.6$ and $\|x - y\|^2 = 0.16 + 0.64 = 0.8 = 2 - 2 \times 0.6$. The Faiss docs give that identity: for normalized vectors $\|x - y\|^2 = 2 - 2\langle x, y\rangle$, so the exact rankings agree. Faiss's recipe for cosine is to normalize database and query vectors with `faiss.normalize_L2` and build the index with `METRIC_INNER_PRODUCT`.

PQ handles inner products with the same table trick, because an inner product also splits into one term per slice. The table entry is the query slice's dot product with each centroid, and scoring is still $m$ lookups and adds, except that larger now means better.

blocks.tex: \langle x, q(y) \rangle = \sum_{j=1}^{m} \big\langle u_j(x),\, q_j(u_j(y)) \big\rangle, \qquad T[j][i] = \langle u_j(x), c_{j,i} \rangle
blocks.caption: Inner-product ADC. No norms, no squares: each slice contributes its dot product with the chosen centroid.

blocks.title: Inner-product lookup table for lesson 3's query and codebooks

scenes.caption: Row j holds the dot product of query slice u_j(x) with each centroid. Example: u1(x) = (0.2, 1.8) with c2 = (0.6, 1.6) gives 0.12 + 2.88 = 3.00.
y0 (0, 3, 2, 0) scores 8.99 and y1 (2, 0, 3, 3) scores 4.68. Largest first: y2, y0, y1, the same order the L2 tables gave.

blocks.md: With an IVF index the stored codes describe the residual $r = y - y_C$, and the inner product splits again: $\langle x, y_C + r\rangle = \langle x, y_C\rangle + \langle x, r\rangle$. The first term is one number per probed list, computed by the coarse search; the second is the usual table, and since $x$ itself does not change per list, one table serves every list. Faiss's fast-scan wiki calls the per-list term the bias.

blocks.prompt: You normalize SIFT10K vectors to unit length and build two 16-byte PQ indexes on the same data: one with L2, one with inner product. Exact L2 and exact inner-product rankings are identical for unit vectors. Will the two PQ indexes return the same top 10?
blocks.reveal: No. We tried it: the top 10 differed for **all 100** queries, and against the true cosine neighbors the L2 index kept **72.8** percent recall@10 while the inner-product index kept **55.6**. The reason is that $\|x - q(y)\|^2 = \|x\|^2 + \|q(y)\|^2 - 2\langle x, q(y)\rangle$, and the reconstruction $q(y)$ is not unit length: its squared norm ranged from 0.62 to 1.17. The inner-product estimate rewards reconstructions that came out long; the L2 estimate charges for it.

blocks.title: Normalized SIFT10K, PQ16: recall@10 vs the true cosine neighbors (%)

scenes.caption: Same codebooks and codes, two scoring rules. L2 ADC 72.8, inner-product ADC 55.6. Ranking by inner product minus half the reconstruction's squared norm reproduces the L2 result exactly.

blocks.md: That measurement is the doorway to ScaNN. The error that hurt was error **along** the data point (the reconstruction came out too long or too short), not error sideways.

**Anisotropic quantization (ScaNN, Scalable Nearest Neighbors).** Anisotropic means not the same in every direction. Guo et al. (ICML 2020, the International Conference on Machine Learning) note that for maximum inner product search (return the database vectors with the largest dot product with the query, the usual score for embeddings), the error that matters is the part that changes the score of high-scoring pairs. Here $x$ is a database point (not the query) and $\tilde x$ its quantized version, so $x - \tilde x$ is the quantization error, not the IVF residual of lesson 5. The score error for a query $q$ is the inner product of $q$ with $x - \tilde x$. The pairs that matter have high scores, so $q$ points roughly along $x$, and then the part of the error along $x$ changes the score most. They split the error $x - \tilde x$ into a component **parallel** to $x$ and one **orthogonal** to it, and show that a score-aware loss weights the parallel part more. Below, the two r terms are those parts and $d$ is the dimension (the $D$ of earlier lessons, not a distance):

blocks.caption: From Guo et al., for the weight function that counts only inner products above a threshold T. With unit-norm data, T = 0.2 and d = 100, eta = 4.125, the value the paper uses on Glove-1.2M.

blocks.md: In words: the loss charges error along $x$ $\eta$ times as much as error across it. The limit says that for large $d$, $\eta$ is about d minus 1, times t squared, divided by 1 minus t squared, where t is $T$ divided by the length of $x$. For unit-norm data with $T = 0.2$ and $d = 100$: $99 \times 0.04 / 0.96 = 4.125$. Glove-1.2M, where the paper uses it, is about 1.2 million 100-dimensional GloVe word vectors (GloVe, Global Vectors, is a word-embedding method from Stanford).

Why does parallel error matter more? A 2-dimensional example computed by script. Take the unit vector $x = (1, 0)$ and two candidate quantizations with the same reconstruction error 0.3: $c_\parallel = (0.7, 0)$, whose error points along $x$, and $c_\perp = (1, 0.3)$, whose error is orthogonal to it. A query that scores high with $x$ points roughly along it, say $q = (0.985, 0.174)$, 10 degrees away from $x$, with true score 0.985.

blocks.title: Two quantizations of x = (1, 0) with equal reconstruction error

scenes.caption: Plain k-means sees no difference: both errors have length 0.3.
Score error for the aligned query: c_par estimates 0.689 (off by 0.295), c_perp estimates 1.037 (off by 0.052). The parallel error is almost fully visible in the score, the orthogonal one barely.

ScaNN's loss with eta = 4.125: 4.125 x 0.09 = 0.371 for c_par, 0.09 for c_perp. The loss prefers c_perp, the paper's Figure 1 point: the closest quantizer is not always the best one for inner products.

blocks.title: How much more ScaNN penalizes parallel error

scenes.caption: At T = 0, every query direction counts equally and the exact eta is 1 (the gray line): ordinary reconstruction loss, which k-means minimizes. The large-d proxy curve reads 0 there, so it is only a guide away from T = 0.
At T = 0.2 with d = 100, parallel error costs 4.125 times as much. Simplified: this uses the large-d limit the paper proposes as a proxy for the exact eta.
Lower d gives a smaller eta at the same T. The codebooks are then learned with this weighted loss instead of plain squared error.

blocks.md: Training keeps the k-means shape. ScaNN alternates an assignment step (pick, for each point, the codeword with the smallest anisotropic loss) and a codebook update; the paper derives the update in closed form, and with $\eta = 1$ it reduces to the ordinary mean. For PQ the same alternation runs over the $M$ sub-codebooks. Search does not change at all: the tables are inner-product tables as above. The anisotropy only decides which codes are stored.

blocks.code:
import numpy as np
import scann

normalized = dataset / np.linalg.norm(dataset, axis=1)[:, np.newaxis]
searcher = scann.scann_ops_pybind.builder(normalized, 10, "dot_product").tree(
    num_leaves=2000, num_leaves_to_search=100, training_sample_size=250000).score_ah(
    2, anisotropic_quantization_threshold=0.2).reorder(100).build()

neighbors, distances = searcher.search_batched(queries)
blocks.caption: Not run here: ScaNN publishes manylinux wheels only (Linux, Python 3.9 to 3.13), per its README. This is the configuration from its example notebook: partition (tree), score with anisotropic PQ over 2-dim blocks (score_ah) using T = 0.2, then re-score the top 100 exactly (reorder).

blocks.md: ScaNN's docs give rules of thumb that match this course: brute force below about 20,000 points; below 100,000, score with AH (asymmetric hashing, its name for ADC over PQ codes) and rescore; above that, partition first, with `num_leaves` near the square root of the number of points; and set `dimensions_per_block` to 2. Rescoring is highly recommended whenever AH is used.

For cosine or inner-product embeddings, measure both L2 and inner-product PQ on your data, and always re-rank: on normalized SIFT10K the scoring rule alone moved recall@10 by 17 points. ScaNN's anisotropic loss is built for exactly this case.

blocks.question: Two codewords reconstruct a unit-norm database vector x with the same squared error. Codeword A's error lies along x, codeword B's is orthogonal to x. For maximum inner product search with T = 0.2, which does ScaNN's loss prefer?
options: A, because error along x keeps the direction of x intact
Either: the errors are equal, so the losses are equal
Neither: ScaNN only uses the threshold during search
B, because parallel error is weighted eta = 4.125 times more and changes the scores of high-scoring queries most
blocks.explain: Queries that score high with x point roughly along it, so their inner product with the error picks up the parallel part almost fully and the orthogonal part barely. The loss weights parallel error by eta (4.125 at T = 0.2, d = 100), so B is preferred even though plain reconstruction error ties.

lessons.title: Beyond slices: residual and additive quantizers

blocks.md: PQ gives each codebook one slice of the dimensions. An **additive quantizer** drops that restriction: each of its $M$ codebooks holds full-length vectors, and a vector is reconstructed as the **sum** of one entry from each. The best-known way to encode is greedy. A **residual quantizer (RQ)** picks the nearest entry of codebook 1, subtracts it, encodes what is left with codebook 2, and so on: each stage refines the error of the previous ones. Lesson 5's IVFADC is already a two-stage version, coarse centroid then PQ code for the residual.

blocks.tex: x \approx x' = T_1[i_1] + T_2[i_2] + \dots + T_M[i_M], \qquad \text{code} = (i_1, \dots, i_M), \quad \textstyle\sum_m \lceil \log_2 K_m \rceil \text{ bits}
blocks.caption: From the Faiss additive quantizer docs. T_m is a table of K_m full-dimensional vectors. PQ is the special case where each table is zero outside its own slice.

blocks.title: Residual quantization of x = (2.6, 1.1) in two stages

scenes.caption: Two 4-entry codebooks over the whole 2-d space (chosen by hand for illustration, not trained): stage 1 is coarse, stage 2 is fine. A code is 2 + 2 = 4 bits.
Residual: x minus (2, 2) is (0.6, -0.9). Stage 2 sees only this. Its entries are (-0.8, 0), (0.8, 0), (0, -0.8), (0, 0.8); squared distances 2.77, 0.85, 0.37, 3.25.
Pick (0, -0.8), index 2. The reconstruction is the sum (2.0, 1.2), code (3, 2). Squared error fell from 1.17 after stage 1 to 0.37 after stage 2.

blocks.md:
The price is encoding. With PQ, slices are independent, so the best code is $M$ separate argmins. With overlapping codebooks, the Faiss paper notes that finding the optimal code is NP-hard (no known algorithm solves every instance efficiently), so encoders use heuristics. Faiss ships two:

- **RQ** encodes stage by stage as above. Greedy choices get trapped in local minima, so it keeps a beam of `max_beam_size` partial codes and picks the best at the last stage. Codebooks are trained stage by stage with k-means.
- **LSQ** (local search quantization, Martinez and others) starts from a rough code and improves it by simulated annealing, randomly flipping codes and re-optimizing; `encode_ils_iters` sets the number of steps.

Search works almost like PQ. Inner products still split per codebook, so a per-query table of $\langle q, T_m[i] \rangle$ gives $\langle q, x' \rangle$ in $M$ lookups. L2 does not split, because the codebook entries overlap and their cross terms do not vanish. Faiss's workaround is to store the reconstruction's squared norm next to the code:

blocks.caption: The norm term is stored per vector, as a float or compressed. The suffix _Nqint8 in a factory string such as RQ15x8_Nqint8 stores it in 8 bits: 15 one-byte codes plus 1 norm byte is 16 bytes.

blocks.md: We compared them with PQ at equal size on SIFT10K: 8 bytes (`PQ8` vs `RQ7x8_Nqint8` and `LSQ7x8_Nqint8`) and 16 bytes (`PQ16` vs `RQ15x8_Nqint8` and `LSQ15x8_Nqint8`), Faiss defaults, trained on the 25,000-vector learning set, exhaustive search. Times are from this Apple Silicon Mac with 2 threads while other jobs ran, so read them as ratios.

blocks.title: SIFT10K at equal code size: PQ vs RQ vs LSQ

scenes.caption: Recall@10 (%). 8 bytes: PQ 58.8, RQ 59.8, LSQ 59.3. 16 bytes: PQ 72.1, RQ 74.8, LSQ 74.3. At 100 queries the 8-byte gains and RQ vs LSQ (0.5 apart) are ties; only the 16-byte gain of 2.2 to 2.7 stands out.

Seconds to encode the 10,000 base vectors. 8 bytes: 0.02, 0.11, 0.69. 16 bytes: 0.11, 0.23, 3.98. LSQ16 encodes 36 times slower than PQ16 here; a rerun gave 67 times, so trust the order of magnitude, not the ratio.
Seconds to train. 8 bytes: 9.9, 8.8, 31.2. 16 bytes: 18.2, 18.4, 152.4. Training LSQ is the expensive step.

blocks.md: Read that honestly. Recall rose a little, but at 16 bytes our reconstruction MSE was not lower (12,481 for RQ and 12,862 for LSQ against 11,168 for PQ), partly because one of the 16 bytes holds the norm. The Faiss authors report the same overall shape at larger scale: additive quantizers are the most accurate option for small codes, PQ remains attractive because encoding is so cheap, and on SIFT1M and Deep1M (1 million image descriptors from a deep network) with IVF the additive variants were clearly more accurate but slower than IVFPQ. Their wiki recommends RQ over LSQ for most uses; the paper finds LSQ more accurate for small codes but not scaling to long ones. Our 8-byte run fits that in MSE (LSQ 21,318, RQ 23,862, PQ 24,754) even though its recall tied RQ's.

The Faiss paper places these quantizers in a strict hierarchy, each able to represent everything the previous one can: binary codes, then scalar quantizers (one dimension per sub-vector), then PQ, then product-additive quantizers (PQ whose slices are each encoded by an additive quantizer, `PRQ16x4x8`), then general additive quantizers. More freedom means better accuracy and more training and encoding cost. At the binary end, RaBitQ quantizes to 1 bit per dimension with an error bound; a later course covers it.

Additive quantizers sum full-dimensional codewords instead of concatenating slices. Decoding is easy, optimal encoding is not, so you pay at index time (beam search or local search) for a few points of recall, and L2 search needs a stored norm.

blocks.question: Why does an L2 index over additive codes store each vector's norm, while PQ does not need one?
options: Because additive codes are signed and PQ codes are not
Because PQ's slices are disjoint, so the squared distance splits into per-slice table entries; overlapping additive codewords leave cross terms, so Faiss uses the norm plus an inner-product table
Because the norm is needed to normalize vectors for cosine similarity
Because additive quantizers cannot compute inner products
blocks.explain: For PQ, the squared distance to a reconstruction is a sum of per-slice squared distances, each in a table. For a sum of overlapping codewords, the squared norm contains pairwise dot products between codewords. Inner products still split, so storing the squared norm of the reconstruction recovers L2 from an inner-product table.

blocks.question: You must re-encode 1 billion vectors every night into 16-byte codes. On our SIFT10K runs, LSQ15x8 encoded tens of times slower than PQ16 (36x once, 67x on a rerun) for about 2 points of recall. Which choice is most defensible?
options: LSQ, because recall always comes first
RQ with the largest possible beam, because the largest beam is always the most accurate
PQ (or RQ with a small beam) plus re-ranking, and measure whether the extra recall survives re-ranking
Binary codes, because they are the top of the quantizer hierarchy
blocks.explain: Encoding time is the limiting factor for additive quantizers, and re-ranking recovers most of the gap between codes anyway (lesson 7). The Faiss wiki also notes that the largest beam is not necessarily the most accurate. Binary codes are the bottom of the hierarchy, not the top.

lessons.title: Sizing and tuning an IVFPQ index for a memory budget

blocks.md: Memory is usually the reason you reach for PQ, so the real job is to turn a budget into an index. Tiny example: 1 million 128-dim vectors as float32 take 512 MB; as `IVF4096,PQ16` they take 16 bytes of code plus an 8-byte id each, 24 MB. This lesson collects the rules for that translation, works one large example, and then tunes the search knobs on a real index.

Start with the curve that drives every sizing decision: how much recall a code size buys. We ran PQ ourselves on synthetic data: 64-dim vectors from 100 Gaussian clusters with a decaying variance spectrum, 10,000 training vectors, 20,000 database vectors and 500 queries, exhaustive search, k-means with 20 iterations (numpy, fixed seed). The metric is **1-recall@10**: the fraction of queries whose true nearest neighbor appears in the top 10, the paper's recall@R with R = 10.

In Faiss names, the first number is M and the second is nbits: `PQ16x8` is 16 sub-quantizers of 8 bits and `PQ32x4` is 32 of 4 bits, both 16 bytes per vector. Lesson 7 showed why 4-bit codes are fast.

blocks.title: 1-recall@10 vs code size (synthetic 64-dim data)

scenes.caption: ADC with 8-bit sub-quantizers (M = 4, 8, 16, 32). Recall climbs steeply with code size: 0.24, 0.42, 0.88, 1.00.
SDC on the same codes: 0.21, 0.33, 0.78, 1.00. Quantizing the query costs recall at every size, most at mid sizes.

ADC with 4-bit sub-quantizers at the same byte budget (M = 8 to 64): 0.24, 0.51, 0.87, 1.00. Similar or better recall here, but on SIFT10K lesson 7 measured PQ32x4 at 61.1 vs 72.1 for PQ16x8; 4-bit wins on speed via SIMD tables.

blocks.md: On real SIFT data the paper found that for a fixed number of bits, fewer sub-quantizers with more centroids generally win, although MSE understates how well many small sub-quantizers do on search. In practice, recall is tuned with code size, nprobe and a **re-ranking** step: fetch more candidates than needed (say 100) using codes, then recompute exact distances for those few from full vectors kept on disk or in a smaller precise code. Faiss exposes this as `IndexRefine` or the `Refine(...)` and `RFlat` factory suffixes. In Faiss, flat means vectors stored uncompressed and compared exactly, so `RFlat` re-ranks with the original vectors.

The Faiss guide to choosing an index gives the rules, mainly for L2:

- **Number of lists.** Below 1M vectors, nlist = $4\sqrt{N}$ to $16\sqrt{N}$. From 1M to 10M use `IVF65536_HNSW32`, from 10M to 100M `IVF262144_HNSW32`, from 100M to 1B `IVF1048576_HNSW32`; the `_HNSW32` suffix finds the nearest coarse centroids with an HNSW graph instead of a scan. `IMI2x9` instead builds an inverted multi-index: a 2-part product quantizer as the coarse quantizer, $2^{18}$ lists, possibly less balanced.
- **Training set.** Between 30 and 256 training vectors per list, the more the better.
- **Encoding by memory pressure.** Somewhat tight: `...,Flat`. Quite tight: `OPQM_D,...,PQMx4fsr`, $M/2$ bytes. Very tight: `OPQM_D,...,PQM`, $M$ bytes, with $M$ typically at most 64 because for larger codes scalar quantization is usually as accurate and faster. Maximum compression: RaBitQ.

A worked example: **100 million 768-dim embeddings on a server with 64 GB of RAM.** As float32 they take 100M x 3,072 bytes = 307.2 GB, so raw vectors are out. Even SQ8 (1 byte per dimension) plus ids is 77.6 GB. The guide's bucket for 10M to 100M is `IVF262144_HNSW32`: $\sqrt{N}$ is 10,000, lists average 381 vectors, and training wants 30 x 262,144 = 7.9M to 256 x 262,144 = 67M vectors. Ids cost 8 bytes each, 0.8 GB: they fit.

blocks.title: 100M x 768 vectors: total RAM per design (GB), budget 64 GB

scenes.caption: Flat vectors with ids: 308 GB. SQ8 with ids: 77.6 GB. Both exceed the budget before any overhead.

A: OPQ64_256,IVF262144_HNSW32,PQ64 is 7.5 GB (64-byte code + 8-byte id, plus 0.27 GB of 256-dim centroids). B: IVF262144_HNSW32,PQ64x4fsr,Refine(SQ4) is 43.3 GB. Both fit; B spends the spare RAM on re-ranking.

blocks.title: Where design B's 43.3 GB goes

scenes.caption: The refine stage dominates: SQ4 keeps 4 bits per dimension, 384 bytes per vector, 38.4 GB. The 32-byte fast-scan codes take 3.2 GB and the ids 0.8 GB.

The index structure is tiny: 262,144 coarse centroids of 768 floats are 0.81 GB, and HNSW32 links over them (32 x 2 links x 4 bytes each) 0.07 GB. Simplified: counts codes and tables only, not allocator slack or query buffers.

blocks.md: Three more checks. The IVFPQ precomputed table from lesson 5 would be 262,144 x 64 x 256 floats, 17.2 GB, far over Faiss's 2 GiB default, so Faiss leaves it off. Exact re-ranking with the float vectors (`RFlat`) would need the 307 GB in RAM, which is why design B refines with a smaller code instead; keeping full vectors on SSD and reading only the shortlist is the DiskANN approach from the previous course. And the Faiss FastScan wiki suggests the same kind of split: from about 64 bytes per vector, give a few bytes to fast-scan codes and the rest to a refinement index (its example: 8 and 56 bytes).

blocks.question: You train `IVF262144_HNSW32,PQ64` on a sample of 2 million vectors. What does Faiss's k-means do, and why?
options: Nothing unusual: 2 million is more than 262,144
It prints a warning asking for at least 10,223,616 training points, because that is 39 per centroid and you have about 7.6
It refuses to train because 2 million is not a multiple of 262,144
It subsamples to 256 points per centroid
blocks.explain: Faiss warns below min_points_per_centroid = 39 per centroid: 39 x 262,144 = 10,223,616. With 7.6 points per list the centroids are noisy and lists unbalanced. The guide asks for 30 to 256 per list; subsampling only happens above 256 per centroid.

blocks.md: Then tune the search. Two knobs matter: `nprobe` (how many lists are scanned) and, with a refine stage, `k_factor` (how many candidates are re-ranked, k x k_factor). Faiss's `ParameterSpace` can set them by name on any index (the refine factor is called `k_factor_rf` there) and can explore combinations for you, keeping only operating points that no faster setting beats. We swept them by hand on SIFT1M (1M vectors, nlist = 4096, 500 queries, one thread, timings from this Mac while other jobs ran). We trained on its 100,000-vector learning set, only 24 per list, so Faiss warned (it wants 159,744): the lesson's own rule, broken knowingly to use the standard split.

blocks.title: SIFT1M, IVF4096,PQ16: sweeping nprobe

scenes.caption: Recall@10 (%) for nprobe 1, 4, 16, 64, 256: 24.3, 39.5, 49.9, 53.0, 53.4. It saturates near 53, the ceiling the 16-byte codes allow (exhaustive PQ16 gave 54.2 on the first 200 of these queries).
Milliseconds per query: 0.039, 0.050, 0.064, 0.158, 0.471. Going from 64 to 256 lists triples the time for 0.4 points.

blocks.title: SIFT1M, IVF4096,PQ32x4fsr,RFlat: nprobe and k_factor together

scenes.caption: nprobe = 64. Recall@10 with k_factor 1, 4, 10: 42.3, 75.6, 89.4 percent at 0.098, 0.086 and 0.094 ms per query. Re-ranking a longer shortlist costs almost nothing here.

nprobe = 256 adds little on top: 76.4 with k_factor 4, 91.2 with k_factor 10, at about 0.25 ms on this run (0.35 to 0.40 on a rerun). Once the lists hold the neighbors, the shortlist length is the knob that pays.

blocks.code:
import time, faiss

index = faiss.index_factory(128, "IVF4096,PQ32x4fsr,RFlat")
index.train(xt); index.add(xb)
ps = faiss.ParameterSpace()

for nprobe in (1, 4, 16, 64, 256):
    for kf in (1, 4, 10):
        ps.set_index_parameters(index, f"nprobe={nprobe},k_factor_rf={kf}")
        t = time.perf_counter()
        D, I = index.search(xq, 10)
        ms = (time.perf_counter() - t) * 1000 / len(xq)
        print(nprobe, kf, recall_at_10(I, gt), round(ms, 3))
blocks.caption: The sweep pattern we ran (our script set index.nprobe and index.k_factor directly). recall_at_10 compares with ground truth from exact search; never tune without it.

blocks.md: PQ also lives inside graph indexes. Faiss's factory builds HNSW over PQ codes (`HNSW32_PQ12`), where the graph links cost 256 bytes per vector at the bottom level, so compressing the vectors saves less than in IVF. DiskANN, from the previous course, keeps only PQ codes in RAM to steer its search and reads full vectors from SSD to re-rank.

Sizing procedure: compute bytes per vector for codes, ids and any refine stage; pick nlist from the guide and train on 30 to 256 vectors per list; then sweep nprobe until recall stops rising, and only then raise k_factor or code size. Measure every point against exact ground truth.

blocks.question: On SIFT1M, IVF4096,PQ32x4fsr,RFlat gives 42.3 percent recall@10 at nprobe 64 with k_factor 1. You need about 90. Which change does our sweep say to try first?
options: Raise nprobe to 256
Retrain with more lists
Switch to 8-bit PQ32
Raise k_factor to 10, so 100 candidates are re-ranked exactly
blocks.explain: At nprobe 64 the lists already contain most true neighbors; the 4-bit codes just rank them poorly. k_factor 10 moved recall to 89.4 at about the same time per query, while nprobe 256 with k_factor 1 reached only 42.4.
